html:
The capture of Jerusalem by a Roman army under Titus in 70 CE, which ended with the burning of the Second Temple. It was the climax of the First Jewish Revolt against Rome, which had begun in 66.

Vespasian led the war until he left to become emperor in 69, handing command to his son Titus. Inside the walls rival Jewish factions fought each other while famine spread. The siege lasted about five months. In late summer the Temple was set on fire, and the city was largely destroyed. Many thousands were killed or sold as slaves. The Jewish historian Josephus, who watched from the Roman side, is the main source. The Arch of Titus in Rome still shows soldiers carrying off the Temple's menorah. The last rebels held out at Masada until 73 or 74.

The loss ended Temple sacrifice and the power of the priests, and the Roman Empire tightened its grip. The rabbis rebuilt Judaism around study, prayer and law, work later written down in the Mishnah. After a final rising, the Bar Kokhba revolt of 132 to 135, Jews were barred from Jerusalem.
